hook.text: HealthSouth's CEO told employees: 'Make the numbers match Wall Street's expectations.'

buildup.text: For seven years, the company fabricated $2.7 billion in fake revenue to meet analyst targets.

discovery.text: Dozens of employees were pressured into making false entries. Refusal meant getting fired.

twist.text: CEO Richard Scrushy claimed he knew nothing. The jury acquitted him—a shocking verdict.

climax.text: He was later convicted of bribery in a separate case and sentenced to seven years.

punchline.text: Meeting Wall Street's number isn't worth prison time.

quiz.question: What drove HealthSouth's accounting fraud?
options: Pressure to meet Wall Street expectations

details.summary: HealthSouth's CEO Richard Scrushy orchestrated a scheme to inflate earnings by $2.7 billion over five years by instructing staff to make fictitious journal entries. This topic covers the fraud mechanics, how it unraveled, and Scrushy's controversial acquittal.
details.whyItMatters: HealthSouth shows how a CEO can override internal controls and pressure subordinates to commit fraud. It highlights the limits of internal controls when tone at the top is corrupt.
takeaways: Scrushy held daily meetings where he told staff exactly how much to inflate earnings to meet Wall Street expectations
Fifteen executives pleaded guilty and testified against Scrushy, who was still acquitted of criminal charges
The fraud was detected when a CFO cooperated with the FBI and wore a wire

faq.question: How did the HealthSouth fraud work?
faq.answer: CEO Richard Scrushy held meetings where he compared actual earnings to Wall Street estimates and directed accounting staff to book fictitious journal entries to close the gap. Over five years, this produced $2.7 billion in fabricated earnings across thousands of fake entries.

faq.question: How was HealthSouth acquitted if fifteen executives testified against the CEO?
faq.answer: Scrushy's defense successfully argued that cooperating executives were lying to save themselves and that no document directly tied him to knowledge of the fraud. The jury acquitted him of all criminal charges, though he was later found liable in a civil SEC lawsuit.
